title: Younger Dryas impact hypothesis
summary: Claim: a fragmented comet or its debris struck/airburst over the Northern Hemisphere ~12,800 years ago, triggering the abrupt Younger Dryas cooling, megafauna extinctions, and the end of the Clovis culture. Evidence offered: platinum spikes, nanodiamonds, microspherules and meltglass at the YD boundary layer across 50+ sites on multiple continents. Proposed by Firestone et al. 2007; still actively defended and attacked in journals as of 2024-2025.

title: Holliday et al., "Comprehensive refutation of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis" (2023)
summary: Earth-Science Reviews paper by Holliday and 15 co-authors: concludes YDIH lacks a self-consistent physical model, that claimed impact markers were not independently reproduced at reliable YD-boundary dates, and that the hypothesis should be rejected. This is the mainstream position's anchor citation.

title: Proponents' 2024 rebuttal: "Rejection of Holliday et al.'s alleged refutation"
summary: A 2024 Earth-Science Reviews reply from YDIH proponents disputes Holliday et al.'s methodology and dating criticisms point by point, calling the 2023 refutation itself flawed. Holliday's group has since counter-rebutted; the exchange is ongoing as of 2024-2025, the textbook definition of a live scientific dispute rather than a settled one.

title: Kennett et al. 2024: shocked quartz and a cosmic-airburst model
summary: UC Santa Barbara's James Kennett and colleagues report shocked, fractured quartz plus platinum, microspherules and meltglass at New Jersey, Maryland and South Carolina sites, dated to the YD boundary. They argue the pressures/temperatures fit a low-altitude airburst rather than a crater-forming impact -- directly answering the standard "where is the crater" critique.

title: Hiawatha crater (Greenland) is 58 million years too old
summary: The one candidate crater proponents pointed to as a possible "smoking gun" was dated by two independent methods (40Ar/39Ar and U-Pb on shocked zircon) to 58 million years ago -- the Late Paleocene, nowhere near the Younger Dryas 12,800 years ago. Published in Science Advances, March 2022.

title: James Kennett on Hiawatha, 2022: "I don't think it's related to the Younger Dryas now"
summary: Kennett, one of YDIH's leading advocates, conceded the Hiawatha dating result and dropped the crater as evidence for his own hypothesis -- a notable case of a proponent updating on disconfirming data rather than dismissing it.

title: Chapman, Morrison & Harris, Skeptical Inquirer, July/Aug 2025: "largely decoupled from mainstream science"
summary: Three planetary-impact scientists write that YDIH "is largely decoupled from multiple mainstream science disciplines...and is accordingly rejected by most experts," citing implausible comet-breakup mechanics ("extraordinarily unlikely that a large comet could break up near Earth and strike it in the way claimed") and poor dating precision at most claimed sites.

title: Climate models: meltwater, not impact winter, best explains the cooling
summary: Nature Geoscience climate modeling finds that even continent-wide wildfires (the proposed impact-winter mechanism) could not generate enough soot to drive Younger Dryas-scale cooling; a North Atlantic meltwater pulse from ice-sheet collapse fits the magnitude and duration far better. The models don't rule out an impact as a possible trigger for that meltwater pulse, but they remove impact winter as the direct cooling mechanism.

title: What would settle the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis
summary: A single impact structure or airburst signature, precisely dated to 12,800 BP by multiple independent labs using multiple methods, with markers (platinum, nanodiamonds, shocked quartz) reproduced by labs outside the original proponent group under blind conditions. Absent that, the dispute stays a live minority position inside real journals -- not settled, not fringe.

title: Lost advanced ice-age civilization (Hancock's case)
summary: Claim (Graham Hancock, Netflix's Ancient Apocalypse, 2022): an advanced global civilization existed before ~11,600 years ago, was destroyed by cataclysm (Hancock links this to the Younger Dryas), and its survivors seeded agriculture, architecture and astronomy into "simple" hunter-gatherers worldwide. Hancock: "I'm not an archaeologist, I'm a journalist investigating human prehistory."

title: Flint Dibble (Cardiff University), The Conversation, Nov 18 2022
summary: Archaeologist's rebuttal published as Ancient Apocalypse aired: the only site Hancock visits that actually dates near the end of the ice age is Gobekli Tepe, and it does not show the advanced global civilization Hancock claims. Dibble also traces Hancock's framework to Ignatius Donnelly's discredited 1882 Atlantis book and to earlier "race science" that credited mysterious outsiders rather than Indigenous peoples for their own monuments.

title: "Apocalypse No!" -- The Nation on pseudo-archaeology's appeal
summary: Long-form critique arguing Hancock's "ancient tech-lords" narrative sells because it flatters a modern audience (a hidden genius civilization like "us") while erasing the actual, well-evidenced achievements of the hunter-gatherers and early farmers who really built these sites.

title: What Gobekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe actually established
summary: Monumental T-shaped-pillar complexes built by hunter-gatherers 9600-8200 BCE, before agriculture or permanent villages were previously thought possible. Karahan Tepe (35km away) adds domestic housing inside a ritual complex, showing organized, large-scale cooperative building among still-foraging populations. This is a real, mainstream-accepted revision to prehistory -- it just doesn't require a prior "advanced civilization": it shows hunter-gatherers were more organized than assumed, not that a lost high-tech culture taught them.

title: Gobekli Tepe in mainstream sequence
summary: Archaeology Magazine's on-site reporting situates Gobekli Tepe within the broader Tas Tepeler cluster of Upper Mesopotamian sites -- part of a documented regional pattern of ritual-then-settlement, not an isolated anomaly requiring outside intervention to explain.

title: Dibble vs Hancock, Joe Rogan Experience, April 2024 -- the four-and-a-half-hour debate
summary: Dibble characterized Hancock as a "pseudoarchaeologist" profiting from sensationalized claims of a lost ice-age civilization without direct evidence; post-debate commentary broadly credited Dibble with the stronger evidentiary case while noting he didn't change Hancock's or Rogan's minds -- illustrating that this fight is now as much cultural/media as scientific.

title: What would settle the lost-civilization claim
summary: A single pre-11,600-BP site with unambiguous markers of advanced civilization -- writing, metallurgy, or engineered monumental architecture beyond hunter-gatherer capability -- independently excavated, dated by multiple labs, and replicated. No such site has been produced in 50+ years of the claim circulating; Gobekli/Karahan Tepe raise the floor on hunter-gatherer capability but do not meet this bar.

title: Ancient astronaut hypothesis
summary: Claim (Erich von Daniken, Chariots of the Gods, 1968; extended by Zecharia Sitchin's Anunnaki mythology): extraterrestrials visited Earth in antiquity and directly created or taught early civilizations, later remembered as gods. Method: touring monuments (pyramids, Nazca Lines, Stonehenge) and asking "coincidence?" about their scale or alignments.

title: Methodology critique: mistranslation and selective evidence
summary: Academic and specialist critiques (Assyriologists, Sumerologists, anthropologists) find Sitchin's Anunnaki-as-astronauts reading rests on disputed, non-standard translations of Sumerian texts and cherry-picked visual "coincidences"; mainstream philology rejects the translations outright, not just the conclusion.

title: Classified as pseudoarchaeology
summary: The ancient astronaut hypothesis is widely categorized by working archaeologists as a form of pseudoarchaeology: it interprets the past while rejecting or misunderstanding standard archaeological method and evidentiary standards, rather than engaging them.

title: Blum & Baumann, The Conversation, March 17 2026: why the belief persists
summary: Two researchers argue persistence rests on "proportionality bias" (extraordinary achievements feel like they need extraordinary causes), institutional distrust ("universities, museums and academic journals are often portrayed as gatekeepers"), and economics: pseudoscientific media is highly profitable while rigorous archaeology is not, so spectacle is simply more visible. Von Daniken's rhetorical trick of posing claims as questions also lets believers feel they reached the conclusion themselves.

title: Media amplification: 15 seasons of Ancient Aliens
summary: The History Channel's Ancient Aliens has run over a decade across 15 seasons, functioning as the theory's main distribution channel to a mass audience largely independent of its reception in archaeology departments.

title: What would settle the ancient astronaut hypothesis
summary: A physical artifact or text, authenticated and independently dated, unambiguously depicting or recording extraterrestrial contact or technology that predates any plausible human origin for it -- verified by independent epigraphers/archaeologists outside the proponent community. None has been produced; every cited example (Nazca Lines, pyramid alignments, Sumerian tablets) has a mainstream non-extraterrestrial explanation that fits the wider evidence base.

title: Catastrophism vs gradualism (the meta-frame)
summary: The 19th-century argument underneath all of the above: does Earth's (and by extension civilization's) history unfold mainly through slow, cumulative, everyday processes (gradualism/uniformitarianism), or through rare, sudden, large-scale catastrophes? Every theory above picks a side implicitly: YDIH and Hancock's lost civilization are catastrophist; mainstream archaeology and geology default to gradualist explanations unless a catastrophe is independently demonstrated.

title: Hutton (1785) and Lyell (1830-33) establish uniformitarianism
summary: James Hutton proposed that ordinary processes -- erosion, sedimentation, uplift -- given enough time, explain the same landforms that catastrophist (flood-based) geology attributed to sudden biblical-scale events. Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology popularized and systematized this, and it became geology's default lens for a century and a half.

title: The modern synthesis: neither pure gradualism nor pure catastrophism
summary: Since the 1980 Alvarez asteroid-extinction hypothesis (Chicxulub) was confirmed, mainstream geology has folded real, sudden catastrophes into an otherwise gradualist framework: Earth's history is slow and cumulative, punctuated by occasional genuine catastrophic events -- each catastrophe judged on its own evidence, not assumed.

title: What would settle a catastrophism-vs-gradualism dispute (in general)
summary: This meta-question is already answered at the framework level (the synthesis above is mainstream consensus); what remains open is case-by-case: for any specific claimed catastrophe (a Younger Dryas impact, a lost civilization's collapse), the same evidentiary bar Chicxulub met -- a dated, physical, independently replicated signature -- either is or isn't met. The frame is settled; each instance is not automatically settled by it.

title: Interdimensional ("ultraterrestrial") UAP hypothesis
summary: Claim (Meade Layne, John Keel, J. Allen Hynek, Jacques Vallee): some UAP are not physical spacecraft from other planets but manifestations of a parallel or higher-dimensional reality that occasionally intersects ours, entangled with human psychology, folklore and even a possible "control system" shaping belief over centuries.

title: Psychosocial UAP hypothesis
summary: Claim: the great majority of UAP/UFO reports resolve to mundane causes (aircraft, balloons, celestial objects, drones) misperceived under an unusual emotional or cultural climate, with the rare unresolved residue better explained by known psychological phenomena (hoaxing, hallucination, social contagion) than by any non-human craft. Occam's razor argument against the extraterrestrial hypothesis.

title: Mick West: most UAP reports are mundane, hyped into a "flap"
summary: Skeptical investigator Mick West's public work argues equipment, drones, balloons and optical/sensor artifacts explain the great majority of viral UAP footage, and that media cycles ("flaps") amplify ambiguous cases faster than they get resolved.

title: AARO FY2025 report (published ~July 21 2026): no evidence of exotic technology
summary: The Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office received 319 UAP reports (June 2024-May 2025), resolved 114 to prosaic causes (balloons, birds, satellites, aircraft, one rocket launch, one jet pack), flagged two cases of unexplained electronic/avionic interference near aircraft, and states it has found no evidence of extraterrestrial activity or technology to date.

title: Pentagon disinformation review: some "UFO" lore was deliberately manufactured
summary: A Department of Defense historical review found the U.S. military deliberately spread UFO rumors -- including staged photos and false briefings -- to protect classified weapons programs during the Cold War. Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick: "These episodes reveal how secrecy and misinformation, even when well-intentioned, can spiral into myth." This complicates both the psychosocial and the exotic-craft accounts: some of the "data" any hypothesis has to explain was manufactured by the government itself.

title: Transparency advocates: "cautiously optimistic ... but concerned"
summary: As the current administration signals a fresh disclosure push, transparency-focused former officials and advocacy groups (context: Christopher Mellon and the Disclosure Foundation) welcome the move but warn classification rules could produce a misleadingly partial release rather than genuine disclosure.

title: What would settle the interdimensional/psychosocial split
summary: Multi-sensor, chain-of-custody physical or instrumented evidence for the small residue of genuinely unresolved cases, reviewed by parties independent of both the claimant community and classified military programs -- so a result can't be waved away as either government cover-up or believer credulity. Until that exists, psychosocial explanations satisfy Occam's razor for the resolved majority, and the unresolved residue remains genuinely open rather than evidence for any specific alternative (interdimensional, exotic craft, or otherwise).

title: A shared tell across all four theories: each one relocates agency away from the people who were actually there
summary: YDIH moves collapse onto an object; Hancock's lost civilization moves achievement onto a vanished teacher, not the hunter-gatherers Gobekli/Karahan Tepe actually document; ancient astronauts move it onto literal visitors; interdimensional UAP moves anomalous experience onto an outside intelligence rather than perception/institutions. Little shared evidence, one shared shape: extraordinary outcome, ordinary people, so an external agent must explain it -- proportionality bias generalized. Name it "agency displacement." Full reasoning: theories/synthesis.md.

title: Kennett'\''s Sept 2025 shocked-quartz paper retracted by PLOS ONE, Feb 2026
summary: The formal peer-reviewed version of the shocked-quartz airburst claim (Murray Springs AZ, Blackwater Draw NM, Arlington Canyon CA; Kennett, LeCompte, Moore, Kletetschka + 13 co-authors, PLOS ONE Sep 2025) was retracted 11 Feb 2026. Editors cited two defects: the radiocarbon age model omitted available samples and included dates centuries before/after the YD onset, and the authors did not sample the full core, so a proxy spike could reflect a change in sedimentation rate rather than a real event.

title: A second Comet Research Group paper (Tall el-Hammam "Sodom" airburst) retracted, April 2025
summary: Scientific Reports formally retracted the 2021 Tall el-Hammam paper (a claimed Tunguska-scale airburst destroying a Bronze Age Jordan Valley city, popularly linked to the Sodom story) on 24 April 2025, after outside reviewers found methodological errors, an unsupported Tunguska comparison, and after the original authors admitted inappropriate image manipulation. Same broader proponent network (Comet Research Group) as the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis; a second retraction inside a year is a real credibility cost, not proof the core YDIH claim is wrong.

title: A third mechanism enters the fight: volcanic forcing (Yobo et al., Science Advances, 29 Apr 2026)
summary: A Texas A&M-led team reports osmium-isotope and siderophile-element data from Florida'\''s Page-Ladson sediment core matching a volcanic-aerosol, not cosmic-impact, signature at the YD onset, and argues deglaciation-driven pressure change naturally increases volcanism at exactly this time. They note platinum spikes elsewhere predate the YD boundary and that a continent-wide impact signature would require implausibly many separate strikes. The paper does not explain the cooling'\''s multi-century duration -- a third proposed trigger alongside impact and meltwater pulse, not a resolution.

title: Holliday'\''s group rebuts the rebuttal: Earth-Science Reviews vol. 258 (2024)
summary: After Sweatman, Powell & West'\''s 2024 reply rejecting Holliday et al.'\''s 2023 refutation, Holliday and co-authors published a direct counter-reply in the same journal restating there is no support for a cosmic-origin catastrophe at ~12,850 cal years BP and standing by their original review. Both sides have now published rebuttal-and-counter-rebuttal pairs in the same peer-reviewed venue -- the shape of a live, unresolved dispute, not a fringe claim being humored by a real journal.

title: Proponents title their own 2024 reply "Rebuttal of Holliday et al.'\''s Comprehensive Gish Gallop"
summary: Sweatman, Powell & West'\''s ScienceOpen reply to Holliday et al. (2023) frames the mainstream review itself as a rhetorical Gish gallop (a barrage of weak arguments meant to overwhelm a responder) rather than engaging it point by point on equal footing -- a framing move common on the losing side of a scientific argument, worth logging because it signals rhetoric doing some of the evidentiary work here.

title: The New York Times, March 2024: "The Comet Strike Theory That Just Won'\''t Die"
summary: Mainstream science journalism'\''s own framing of YDIH'\''s persistence -- neither dismissing it as settled pseudoscience nor treating it as accepted, but naming its unusual durability across nearly two decades of published rebuttal, and noting the debate reads to outsiders as much like an identity fight as a scientific one.

title: What the 2026 retractions actually change: they close two flawed data points, not the argument
summary: Neither the Sept 2025 shocked-quartz retraction (originally covering Murray Springs, Blackwater Draw, Arlington Canyon) nor the 2025 Tall el-Hammam retraction touches the platinum/nanodiamond/microspherule record claimed at 50+ other cited sites, and Holliday'\''s side has never claimed the retractions as proof the core hypothesis is false, only that specific proponent papers failed peer scrutiny. What would move this further: an independent, non-Comet-Research-Group lab replicating a marker at a precisely YD-dated site under blind conditions -- the same bar round 1 named, still not met by either side in 2026.

title: Karahan Tepe, Oct 2025: first human face ever carved directly onto a T-shaped pillar
summary: A 135cm standing stone with a detailed carved human face (deep-set eyes, prominent nose, angular jaw) was uncovered at Karahan Tepe in October 2025 -- the first time a literal face has appeared on one of the anonymous T-shaped pillars that define the Tas Tepeler culture. A second, matching statue followed weeks later. Excavation director Necmi Karul (Istanbul University) reads the growing run of human sculpture as a direct outcome of settled life, not an outside influence.

title: Gobekli Tepe: a life-size human statue found built directly into a wall between two structures
summary: Alongside Karahan Tepe'\''s new face-pillar, excavators at Gobekli Tepe found a life-size human statue deliberately embedded into a stone wall between Structures B and D -- more evidence that explicit human representation, not just abstract T-pillar symbolism, was part of the site'\''s own design across its building phases, not introduced from outside.

title: Karahan Tepe, Oct 2025: 30+ Neolithic dwellings found beneath the ritual sanctuary level
summary: Excavation exposed more than 30 domestic dwellings under Karahan Tepe'\''s sanctuary layer, reframing the site as one of the world'\''s first villages rather than a ritual center built by itinerant foragers with no settled base of their own -- the opposite direction from the lost-civilization argument, which needs foragers who could not have organized this themselves.

title: The Tas Tepeler cluster keeps growing: Ayanlar Hoyuk, Sefer Tepe and Sayburc all added 2025-2026
summary: Round 1 already noted Gobekli Tepe sits inside a documented regional pattern (Tas Tepeler), not an isolated anomaly. Since then: Sayburc yielded a statue with a deliberately stitched mouth (Dec 2025); Sefer Tepe produced carved human faces on a platform plus a double-faced bead (Feb 2026); Ayanlar Hoyuk confirmed the same Neolithic cultural sphere at a new location (Apr 2026). Each addition widens the known network of ordinary, settled, symbol-making communities -- the opposite of a single point-source teaching culture.

title: The oldest confirmed Gobekli Tepe date (Enclosure D, ~9530 BCE) has not moved outside the known window
summary: Martin Sweatman'\''s dating work on Enclosure D, the site'\''s largest uncovered structure, produced the oldest radiocarbon date yet measured there: roughly 9530 BCE -- inside, not before, the 9600-8200 BCE range round 1 already reported. New 2025-2026 finds add sophistication and scale, not an earlier start date; the lost-civilization argument needs an earlier date more than it needs more art, and that has not arrived.

title: A mainstream-adjacent academic makes his own catastrophist reading: Sweatman'\''s comet-calendar pillar (2024)
summary: Martin Sweatman (University of Edinburgh) published in Time and Mind (24 Jul 2024) that Pillar 43'\''s V-shaped marks encode a 365-day lunisolar calendar and record a comet impact around 10,850 BCE -- his own YDIH-proponent reading of Gobekli Tepe'\''s art. Worth separating from Hancock: Sweatman is a credentialed, publishing YDIH advocate making one specific, falsifiable claim about one pillar, not a general lost-teacher-civilization claim -- and he is separately on record rejecting Hancock'\''s broader observatory and star-map framing of the same site.

title: Karul, Notroff and Sweatman on record, Dec 2024: no observatory evidence, no star map
summary: A Turkiye Today debunking piece quotes excavation director Necmi Karul, researcher Jens Notroff and Martin Sweatman rejecting the specific claims that Gobekli Tepe functioned as an astronomical observatory or that Pillar 43 depicts a star map -- noting surviving wooden traces show the structures were roofed, and that the vulture-and-skull imagery fits documented Neolithic Anatolian death-ritual practice. The pushback targets Hancock'\''s specific readings, not the site'\''s genuine, separately-documented sophistication.

title: Karahan Tepe, Feb 2026: a modest stone staircase reassessed as possibly the world'\''s oldest
summary: A previously unremarkable stone staircase at Karahan Tepe is being reconsidered by excavators as potentially the oldest known staircase, which would push back the earliest evidence of engineered vertical movement in architecture. As of this writing this is a reassessment in progress, not a settled dating claim -- logged here as a live thread, not a fact, and it still sits inside the known site chronology either way.

title: Proportionality bias, precisely: big events need big causes (McCauley & Jacques 1979; Brotherton)
summary: The mechanism round 1'\''s Blum & Baumann citation named for ancient astronauts has its own academic home: proportionality bias (McCauley & Jacques 1979; popularized by psychologist Rob Brotherton) is documented conspiracy-theory-psychology literature, most famously applied to JFK-assassination theories, and a 2025 Journal of Economic Surveys review groups it with agency-detection bias and the conjunction fallacy among the standard cognitive biases behind conspiracy belief generally. This is the established academic anchor '\''agency displacement'\'' would sit on top of, not a novel mechanism itself.

title: Hyperactive agency detection (HADD, Justin Barrett) is a cousin, not the same claim
summary: Barrett'\''s HADD (cognitive science of religion, since 2000) argues human minds are tuned to over-detect agents in ambiguous stimuli -- a shape in the bushes reads as a predator, not the wind -- because false positives cost less than false negatives. This explains why people reach for an agent explanation at all; it does not explain why they reach for an outside agent over the people already known to be present, which is the specific move '\''agency displacement'\'' names. Related, not identical: HADD is about detecting agency, agency displacement is about relocating it.

title: The closest real match already has a name and a century of criticism: hyperdiffusionism
summary: Archaeology'\''s own term for crediting a single outside or superior culture rather than the people who were actually there is hyperdiffusionism -- most infamously the 19th/20th-century Mound Builder myth, which denied North American Indigenous peoples built their own earthworks. Historians of pseudoarchaeology (Kenneth Feder, Jason Colavito) have documented this pattern for decades and tied it explicitly to colonialism and racism, not just bad evidence. '\''Agency displacement,'\'' applied to a single domain, is this pattern under a new name.

title: Round 1'\''s own log already named this pattern -- the speculation label undersold the archaeology half
summary: Re-reading round 1: entry 11 (Dibble, The Conversation, Nov 2022) already says Hancock'\''s framework traces to Ignatius Donnelly'\''s Atlantis book and to earlier '\''race science'\'' that credited mysterious outsiders rather than the Indigenous peoples who actually built these sites. That is the archaeological case for '\''agency displacement,'\'' sourced, sitting inside round 1'\''s own established-credence material. The synthesis'\''s '\''original observation'\'' framing held for the four-theory generalization, not for the archaeology-specific mechanism, which was already on the very page it was drawn from.

title: Stress-test verdict: rediscovery at the archaeology layer, an untested generalization above it
summary: Naming a claim does not retroactively invent it: the narrow claim (pseudoarchaeology denies the real builders'\'' agency and gives it to an outsider) is a rediscovery of hyperdiffusionism, a century-old, well-documented pattern. What no single source in this round'\''s searching combines is the four-domain generalization -- an impact'\''s cause displaced onto a comet, a monument'\''s onto a vanished teacher, a text'\''s onto literal visitors, an experience'\''s onto another reality -- as one shared move spanning geology, archaeology and ufology at once. Not refuted by anything found either; simply untested, which is what speculation is for.

title: SNARC is a real, unrelated effect -- a dead end for this stress-test, logged so nobody re-walks it
summary: The brief named '\''SNARC-style narrative studies'\'' as an avenue; SNARC (spatial-numerical association of response codes, Dehaene et al. 1993, still actively studied per a 2026 Scientific Reports methods paper) is a genuine cognitive-psychology effect about how the mind maps numbers onto left/right space -- unconnected to narrative bias, agency attribution, or conspiracy belief. Narrative bias (trusting stories over data) is the real neighboring term and was checked separately; it does not name this pattern either. Recorded so a future round does not spend a search on the same false lead.

title: Lead author Nana Yobo vs. an outside reviewer on the volcanic paper: real signal, not the whole story
summary: Texas A&M'\''s Lucien Nana Yobo says impact evidence has remained limited and difficult to reproduce while their volcanic signal is clear and consistent across multiple sites and ice cores. An outside researcher reviewing the same paper was more measured: I don'\''t think it fully explains the Younger Dryas, but it could be part of the explanation -- this looks like solid geological work. Neither claims the debate is over; the volcanic camp is now a third named party, not a tiebreaker between the other two.

title: What would falsify agency displacement as a real, generalizable pattern (not just wordplay)
summary: A pre-registered content analysis coding a representative sample of fringe/catastrophist claims across domains (not hand-picked to fit) for whether they structurally relocate agency from a documented group onto an undocumented outside one, compared against a matched sample of fringe claims that do NOT do this. If the displacement structure shows up no more often than chance in fringe claims generally, the pattern is an artifact of these four cherry-picked examples, not a real bias. Nobody has run this test; until then the generalization stays speculation, correctly labeled.

title: The rate at which AI search invents citations, measured: wrong more than 60% of the time
summary: Klaudia Jazwinska and Aisvarya Chandrasekar, Tow Center for Digital Journalism, 6 March 2025: 1,600 queries across eight AI search tools (ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, Perplexity Pro, DeepSeek, Copilot, Grok-2, Grok-3, Gemini) returned incorrect answers to more than 60 percent of queries -- 37% for Perplexity, 94% for Grok 3. More than half of Gemini and Grok 3 responses cited fabricated or broken URLs; 154 of Grok 3s citations led to error pages. And the tools rarely hedged: ChatGPT misidentified 134 of 200 articles while signalling low confidence just 15 times. This program caught two invented citations by hand; that is the population they came from.

title: The failure mode is older than AI and already named: circular reporting, or citogenesis
summary: A claim with no source is repeated by an outlet, the outlet is then cited as the source, and the loop closes -- circular reporting, nicknamed citogenesis after Randall Munroes xkcd 978 (November 2011). Wikipedia maintains a list of documented incidents on its own pages, including a 2007 fabrication about Sacha Baron Cohen and Goldman Sachs that real newspapers repeated. AI search does not introduce this failure; it removes the friction that used to slow it down, because the loop now closes in one query instead of one news cycle. The defence is unchanged and cheap: fetch the cited page and read it.

title: Why the cheap decisive experiment does not get run: replication funding is near zero
summary: Brian Nosek (Center for Open Science) told Undark in September 2017 that US funding for replication is near zero, and that one or two percent of research budgets devoted to replication might be enough to really balance the efforts against novelty work. The reported barriers are structural, not technical: prestigious journals rarely publish replications, the work does not earn tenure, and re-testing a colleagues result carries a social cost. This is the general mechanism behind every what-would-settle-it answer in this program that ends nobody has done it -- the missing step is almost never hard or expensive, it is unrewarded.

title: Four of this programs load-bearing disputes each rest on exactly one unreplicated measurement
summary: Reading all four logs together: Dunns Serapeum flatness figures (1995/2001, never re-measured by anyone), Qvists OG Vase radial deviations (2023, reversed by the same author in 2025 once a better scan existed), the Princeton radar tracks behind Knuths 5,370g figure (2019, raw data never released by either side), and the Comet Research Groups platinum/nanodiamond markers (no blind replication outside the proponent group in 19 years). Each is the load-bearing number in its dispute; each has been produced once. This is a reading of the logs, not a claim anyone else has made -- but it is checkable line by line.

title: ROUND 4 Q1: why has nobody pointed an instrument at the object?
summary: In three topics the decisive measurement is cheap, permitted and unperformed. The Serapeum boxes and the Giza coffer: site open since 2012, sub-centimetre laser scanning already running at Saqqara in 2026, roughly 170 foreign missions holding Egyptian permits. The Nimitz radar: both Knuths team and Mick West say released multi-sensor data would settle it. The Younger Dryas markers: no blind out-of-group replication since 2007. What would settle it: one named institution funding and publishing one of the three -- or a documented account of the specific funding or permit path that fails, tested against Noseks near-zero-replication-funding explanation.

title: ROUND 4 Q2: does agency displacement survive a pre-registered test, now that there are six instances?
summary: Round 2 stress-tested the pattern and landed on an honest split: at the archaeology layer it is a rediscovery of hyperdiffusionism, a century old and well documented; the cross-domain generalization is untested. Round 3 adds two more instances from sibling topics that were never pointed at it -- stones lost-technology framing displaces Egyptian and Andean masons, depictions outsider readings displace the Camunni, the Worrora and the Hopi. Six instances is still a hand-picked six. What would settle it is unchanged and nobody has run it: a pre-registered content analysis over a representative sample of fringe claims, against a matched sample that does not displace agency.

title: ROUND 4 Q3: is the recency signature a signature, or is it what every tradition looks like?
summary: Four claimed-ancient traditions -- Blue Star Kachina, Dogon Sirius, the Emerald Tablets, the Kolbrin -- all first document in the 20th century, and Hobsbawm and Rangers invented tradition names the category. But four cases chosen because they looked suspicious cannot establish a base rate. What would settle it: code a sample that includes traditions which genuinely ARE ancient and have manuscript attestation, scoring each on the gap between claimed origin and earliest documented appearance, and check whether the fringe subset separates from the rest. If real traditions show the same gap, the signature is an artifact of who gets audited.

title: ROUND 4 Q4: how much of what this program read was machine-invented?
summary: Two fabricated citations were caught in round 2, both the same way -- fetching the page the search summary cited and finding the claim absent: a Digital Saqqara Project that does not exist, and a Stocks sawing figure not on the PBS page it was attributed to. Both were found by accident while chasing something else, so the denominator is unknown, and the Tow Center measured AI search citations wrong in over 60% of 1,600 queries. What would settle it: fetch every url in all four logs, check that the specific figure each entry attributes to it appears on the page, and publish the failure rate. The program can audit itself; nothing external is required.

title: ROUND 4 Q5: does "resolved" mean the same thing in any two of these four topics?
summary: AARO grades each closed case -- Al Taqaddum high confidence, Eglin moderate -- then reports 114 of 319 resolved with no grade attached. Archaeology has no such vocabulary at all: Stocks measured granite removal at 5.2 cm3/hour, which is a demonstrated mechanism, while the Mauryan polish is called by its own mainstream sources one of the genuine unsolved problems of ancient technology -- and both sit under explained. What would settle it: apply one explicit confidence vocabulary, ICD 203s or another, to every mainstream explanation across all four topics and publish which ones drop a level. The disagreement it would expose is inside the mainstream, not between mainstream and fringe.
